Hoshi Valley, on the last train of winter. Kobo, the little red valley engine, wheezes to a stop.
Hoshi Station! End of the line, and the end of my patience with this cold.
…You must be Sora's granddaughter. Mika, isn't it?
That's me. You're Genzo? Grandma's letters said you'd be grumpy.
Hah! She wasn't wrong. You have her eyes, you know. Don't…
…Well. Here. The key to her cottage. It's up the bluff, by the viaduct.
Mind the fallen fence. And don't go poking at that bridge.
Grandma's cottage… it smells like cedar and old tea.
There was a chest by the porch in all her photos.
Inside the chest: a brass signal lantern with red glass, every letter Mika ever sent, and a note with her name on it.
A little gold light has tumbled out of the lantern. It is… snoring?
…mmh. Five more minutes, Sora…
!!! You are NOT Sora! Who are you? Where am I? Why is it so BRIGHT?
Whoa—you're a… star? A talking star?
I'm a hoshibi! A star-fire! I'm Tamo! I think. Probably. It's all very fuzzy.
I remember a lamp… and rain… and then a really long nap.
There's a note from Grandma. Let's read it.
Mika — if you are reading this, I am gone, and you have met Tamo. Be patient with him; he is braver than he looks.
The valley has four Star Lamps: Forest, Mill, Orchard and Viaduct. Ten years ago they went dark, and the Star Train stopped coming.
On star-fall night, that train carried the whole valley across the viaduct, together. Bring it home before the stars fall this winter.
Light the four lamps again. Start with the Mill Lamp, down in Kawabe.
And Mika: don't be angry with Genzo. He has carried enough.
…Oh, Grandma. And why would I be angry with Genzo?
Sora's… gone? Oh. …Then I'll help you. I'm very good with lamps. I think. Watch this!
Walk up to the porch lamp and press {act}. I'll do the rest. Pfft—like a sneeze, but useful!
I did it! Did you see? Pfft! Spark! I am SO good at this.
So that's how the lamps get lit. Grandma says to start with the Mill Lamp, down in Kawabe.
Kawabe! The river village! Let's go! …Which way is Kawabe?
Hey! You're standing on my fishing spot. Also you're scaring the trout.
Sorry. I'm Mika, Sora's granddaughter. I'm looking for the Mill Lamp keeper.
…Sora's granddaughter? Oh. I'm sorry. The keeper's my grandpa, Ōta. He won't let you near that lamp.
Nobody touches it. Not since the flood. And that was Takamori's fault anyway.
Takamori's fault?
The orchard village, across the river. Their lamp stayed lit when it should've gone dark. Grandpa says so. A lot. Every day.
Go try him. He's at the mill, upriver. Don't say I didn't warn you.
Hm? A city girl in a raincoat. Go home. The mill is closed. The lamp is closed. Everything is closed.

…Sora's.

He said no, right? Classic Grandpa.
Okay. Plan. Grandpa melts for grilled trout. Catch me three fish—any fish, we'll call them trout—and I'll grill them.
Rod's on the dock. Cast, wait for the float to dip, then press {act}. That's all there is to it.
Three! Not bad for a city girl. Okay, maybe good. Don't let it go to your head.
I'll grill these. Take the plate to Grandpa—say it was your idea.
…Is that grilled trout?

Get close and press {act}. I'll give it a little boop—just enough to make it drop the cog.
Boop! Ha! It dropped it! It looks very offended. Sorry, Mr. Crab!
Three cogs! Let's fix that wheel!
The cogs slide into place. The old axle groans, shudders… and the great wheel turns.
…It turns. Ten years, and it turns.

s: There goes the drawbridge. The island's yours, Sora's girl. Light it at sundown—that's when a lamp earns its keep.

s: The lamp! It's… it's so warm. I remember this. I remember lamps.
I remember… lanterns, and someone shouting. The river was so loud.
Tamo? Are you okay?
I'm okay. It's just a memory. A loud one.
Look at it. The Mill Lamp, burning again. Sora would…

s: She left this with me, a page of her journal. I never had the heart to read it. Here. It's yours.

s: Forest, Mill, Orchard, Viaduct. If one lamp goes dark, the next must go dark. A lit lamp says all clear; a dark lamp says stop.
The next lamp downriver is Takamori's. Rin will ferry you over. Go and see what they have to say for themselves.
ctx: dialogue c1_ota_page, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: Takamori! Look at all those peach trees. The Orchard Lamp must be up there somewhere.
Kawabe says the flood was Takamori's fault. Let's hear what Takamori says.
Ooh, the other side of the story. Every story has one. Some have three.
Oh! A new face! Here, have a peach bun, you look half-starved. Who are you, sweetheart?
Mika. Sora's granddaughter. I came about the Orchard Lamp.
…Sora's. Oh, love. I was so sorry to hear.
And you came across the river… so Ōta sent you. Let me guess what he told you. That it was our fault.
Well, here's the truth: the Mill Lamp stayed lit that night. Kawabe was down here drinking at our festival.
He says exactly the same thing about you.
Does he now. Hmph.
The lamp's up in the bell tower and the key's in my apron. But the summer fair is tomorrow, and it's a disaster.
My sheep are loose, the crows are at my peaches, and the fair basket down the orchard lane still needs five ripe ones.
Help me save my fair and the key is yours. Sheep first—walk up to each one and it'll trot home to the pen.
All five home! You're a natural, Mika. Next on Hana's list: the crows.
The scarecrow bells scare them off, but nobody can reach them. Nobody except a very talented star! Ding-ding!
Listen to that! Not a crow left. Now five ripe peaches for Hana's fair basket.
The peaches go into Hana's fair basket. Tucked under its cloth: a warm peach bun and a note.
For Genzo at the station, if you'd be a dear. He used to come by every week. After that night, he stopped coming anywhere.
A peach bun. From Hana.
…Take it back. Tell her… tell her I don't deserve Hana's buns.
Genzo, what happened that night?
The river happened. Go on, now. Train's leaving.
(whispering) He's sad-grumpy. That's different from hungry-grumpy.
He wouldn't take it? …No. I suppose he wouldn't.
Here's the key, love. Climb up and ring the bell for me—it's been too quiet—then light that lamp.
BONG. The old bell rolls across the valley, and every bird in Takamori takes off at once.
That was LOUD! Do it again! No—look, the sun's going down. The lamp's right above us. Press {act}!
The Orchard Lamp! Oh… another memory.
The train was so bright. It was coming, and coming… and it didn't slow down.
The Star Train? It didn't slow down? But the lamps were supposed to warn it.
I don't know. It's all fog after that.
It's lit. It's really lit. Here—Sora gave me this years ago. Said I'd know when to pass it on.
Ōta and Hana were both at the festival that night. So was I, until I heard the river.
The Forest Lamp is up at the shrine. I've opened the upper orchard gate for you. Nobody's gone up since Old Kiku left.
Mika! A fox! A fox in a little red bib! It wants us to follow it!
That's a shrine bib, and it's stitched 'Kon'. He must be the shrine's fox.
Oh no. Oh no no no. That is the biggest bear in the whole world and it's asleep ON the stairs.
There's a note on the shrine board. From Old Kiku.
To whoever comes after me: if Ōkuma sleeps on the steps, the forest is still sad. Feed him something sweet.

s: He is fond of honey chestnuts. Three chestnuts, two mushrooms, one honeycomb, and a little patience at the pot.
ctx: dialogue c3_bear, spoken by Old Kiku

s: A bear recipe! We can do that. Probably. The bees might not like it.
Honey means bees, and bees mean a hive. There's one hanging on a branch east of the chestnuts.
Walk under it and press {act}. One good spark and it'll drop… and then we RUN.
It dropped! Grab the honeycomb! Bees! BEES! Run, Mika!
It smells like autumn in a bowl. If I had a stomach, it would be growling.
Mika, look across the river. Half that hillside is missing. Can we look? The bear isn't going anywhere.
Look at this slope. The whole hillside slid into the river.
It must have dammed the river, then burst. That was the flood. Nobody caused it—not Kawabe, not Takamori.
Nobody broke the river. The river broke itself.
Ōkuma sniffs the bowl… opens one enormous eye… and eats the whole thing in a single, happy gulp.
He yawns, stretches, pats Mika very gently on the head, and ambles off into the maples.
He PATTED you! That is the greatest thing that has ever happened!
The Forest Lamp! I remember… I remember the whole night now. Almost.
Sora ran onto the viaduct with me in her lantern. She was waving it. Red. Red. Red.
And the train was so loud. And in the engine's window… Genzo. I remember Genzo's face.
Genzo was driving the Star Train that night.
Tucked behind the Forest Lamp, where Old Kiku kept it safe: journal page 3, in Sora's hand.
Old Kiku put her lamp out that night. She did her part. The rest of us didn't.
Winter. Snow on the rails, and the stars fall tomorrow night.
One lamp left, on a bridge with a hole in it. And one person who knows what really happened.
Genzo. In this snow he'll be in the engine shed. Let's go.
Sora's lantern. And… that little light. I'd know it anywhere.
You. You were driving. Sora put the Viaduct Lamp out—she scooped me into her lantern—and you didn't stop.
The Mill and Orchard Lamps both said 'clear'. I thought the wind had blown hers out.
Then she was on the tracks, swinging that red lantern like a mad thing. I pulled the brake so hard I tore my shoulder.
We stopped four metres from where the span fell. Forty people. All alive. Because of her.
She was still on the viaduct when it went. She never walked right again. Because of me.
Kawabe blames Takamori. Takamori blames Kawabe. And I let them. Because it was easier than the truth.
Grandma's letter said not to be angry with you. She said you'd carried enough.
…She would say that. She gave me this before she died. Sealed, for you. I opened it. I've read it every day since.
Genzo, you old snoop, of course you read this. I forgave you before the train stopped rolling. Now forgive yourself.
"You have to tell them yourself."
"Grandma forgave you. We'll tell them together."
…Yes. Yes, I do. It should be me. Tonight, on the platform. Bring Ōta and Hana.
Together. …She'd have liked that. Tonight, on the platform. Bring Ōta and Hana.
A meeting? At the station? With HER? …Fine. For Sora's girl. Only for Sora's girl.
ctx: dialogue c4_gather_ota, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: Ōta will be there? …Then I'm bringing a very large basket of buns. For courage.
Snow falls on Hoshi Station. Kawabe stands on one side of the platform, Takamori on the other.
Everyone. Please. I have something I should have said ten years ago.
The Viaduct Lamp was dark that night. Sora put it out, like she was supposed to. I saw it, and I didn't stop.
It was my fault. Not Kawabe's. Not Takamori's. Mine.
Everyone—Genzo and I have something to tell you. About the night the Star Train stopped.
The Viaduct Lamp was dark. Sora did her part. I saw it, and I didn't stop. That's on me.
And Grandma forgave him. She wrote it down—it's the last page of her journal.
…My Mill Lamp was lit that night because I was at Takamori's festival. Drinking. Not watching.
ctx: dialogue c4_meeting_after, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: And my Orchard Lamp was lit because I was selling buns. Not watching either.
So… nobody's the villain? That's somehow worse.
No! That's BETTER! It means everybody can fix it!
…Hana. The mill still has timber seasoned for that span.
ctx: dialogue c4_meeting_after, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: And Takamori's smithy has the bolts. Has had them for ten years.
Then. Tomorrow.
ctx: dialogue c4_meeting_after, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: Tomorrow.
Timber from Kawabe, iron from Takamori, and a girl with a hammer. The viaduct, first thing, Mika.
Morning. Genzo is already up on the viaduct with the Kawabe timber and the Takamori iron.
Three new beams across the gap, Mika! You swing the hammer. I'll do the cheering.
Solid as the day she was built. Better, maybe.
Tonight the stars fall. Go and light that lamp—Kobo doesn't cross until all four say 'clear'.
Mika. All four. Forest, Mill, Orchard… Viaduct. Look at them.
I remember everything now. And I remember where I belong.
All aboard the Star Train! Kawabe AND Takamori! No pushing! Ōta, that means you!
Mika—up front with me. Press {act} as each trackside lantern comes near. Show them the way home.
The Star Train rolls into Takamori Halt as the sky begins to fall—one star, then ten, then a thousand.
Mika. The Viaduct Lamp was my lamp, before Sora carried me off to keep me safe. It needs its hoshibi. It needs me.
You're going back into the lamp.
I'll keep watch. Every night. You keep watch too, okay? That's how lights work. Somebody has to be looking.
…Okay. I'll keep watch. Goodnight, Tamo.
Spring comes back to Hoshi Valley. The Star Train runs every Sunday now.
Kawabe and Takamori share one festival, on the viaduct, and argue about the buns.
And Sora's cottage has a new Viaduct Lamp keeper—who waves at a small gold light every night.
On Sundays, Genzo tells his passengers the whole story himself. "First brave thing I did in ten years," he says. "Felt like breathing."
On Sundays, Genzo saves Mika the seat up front. "You stood by me on that platform," he says. "She'd be proud of you."
Mika—if you found all twelve fallen stars, you walked every corner of my valley. Good.
Here is my secret: I never lit the lamps for the train. I lit them so someone would look up.
Keep looking up, my darling. Love, Grandma.
Hold on to something! Ferry's leaving!
The ferry's frozen in till spring! Good news: the whole river is a road now. A slippery road.
Frozen in till spring. Fine, I'll walk across. Carefully. Mostly.
Ferry? Not a chance. Grandpa says nobody crosses until the Mill Lamp's lit.
The orchard gate is locked tight. Hana has the key to everything up here.
The drawbridge is up. It lifts with the mill wheel, and the wheel isn't turning.
The bell-tower door is locked. Hana has the key.
That's where the span fell. Don't even THINK about jumping.
The bear is asleep across the whole staircase. We can't get past. We need a plan. And maybe a snack.
The light runs down the river like a wave, and every cherry tree in Kawabe blooms at once.
Grandpa! GRANDPA! The koi are jumping! Right over the wheel!
…Hah. Hahaha! Ten years, and this valley still knows how to throw a party.
ctx: dialogue c1_party, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: A rainbow! And look, Mika, the petals are making a star. It points across the river!
To Takamori. Then that's where we're going next.
The bell's last note rolls over the orchard, and every peach tree lights up like a paper lantern.
Fireflies! Thousands of them! Somebody fetch the drums. The summer festival starts NOW!
I may have sparked a little too hard. …Why are the sheep floating?
Never mind the sheep, sweetheart. Dance!
Down on the river, one small lantern boat drifts over from Kawabe. Nobody from Kawabe is waving. Somebody sent it anyway.
…Well, well. The old radish.
The Forest Lamp flares gold, and the whole wood answers.
Kodama! Forest spirits, hundreds of them! They're rattling their heads. That means hello!
The maple leaves let go of their branches and flutter up the shrine steps as golden butterflies.
Somewhere on the wind, an old woman laughs, pleased.
Look who came. Ōkuma, Kon, the deer… everyone.
It's a moon-viewing! Everybody sit! Kon, no, that's MY dumpling!
Then the falling stars gather, one by one, into a train of light that crosses the whole sky.
That's… the Star Train. And in the window… Sora. She's waving. She's waving at us.
Of course she is. She always waved first.

s: Well, wave back, you two old fools! Everybody wave!
Three buns each. No arguments. Genzo, Ōta: shake hands. Properly.
…Friends, then?
Friends. You still owe me ten years of radish.
ctx: dialogue c4_photo, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: Photo! Everybody squash in on Kobo! Grandpa, smile. Genzo, you too!
I AM smiling.
Same time next year?
Same time next year.
ctx: dialogue c4_photo, spoken by Grandpa Ōta

s: Mika! MIKA! Guess what! The lamp says I get Sundays off!
Tamo! …Wait. Is it Sunday?
It's Sunday if you say it fast enough! Come on, the whole valley's waiting!
Psst. Sora hid more than stars, you know. Letters on the rooftops, a music box, keepsakes in every home…
Want to go treasure hunting too? I can make them twinkle for you!
"Yes! Let's find every treasure!"
"Just the stars for now."
The stars are home! But Sora's treasures are still hiding out there. One last adventure?
"Not now. I just want to wander."
Treasure hunt! Look for the little twinkles. Find the stars first, then my arrow will lead you to every treasure left.
Treasure hunt! Follow the arrow: I'll point you to every treasure left, one by one.
Okay! If you change your mind, it's in the journal: Treasures, Start the treasure hunt.
That's EVERY treasure. Every letter, every keepsake, the music box, the kite, the tree… Sora would be so proud.
She hid them for me to find. And I found all of them.
Sora's kite rests here when we're not flying. Out in the open, call it with the Kite button (G), and off we go!
Grandma's kite rests here when I'm not flying. Outside, the Kite button (G) calls it.
Sora's music box. Inside, a tiny Kobo circles a tiny track, and the lullaby she used to hum begins to play.
For a moment the riverbank fills with golden light: four young friends, dancing at the Star Train festival.
Grandma… and Genzo, Ōta and Hana. Look how happy they were.
They still can be. That's what the lamps are for.
Grandma… and Genzo, Ōta and Hana. Look how happy they were. Look how happy they are again.
Ōkuma pads over and drops something shiny at Mika's feet: a golden acorn.
A thank-you present! Plant it somewhere special, Mika.
Somewhere special… Grandma's garden.
Mika presses the golden acorn into the soil of Sora's garden. The ground glows, and something stirs.
A young tree rises up in a spiral of light, its leaves shining like small stars.
A star-tree! Sora would have LOVED this. I love this. I live here now.
A star-tree, in Grandma's garden. She would have loved this.
Something heavy is tangled in the line: a brass pocket compass whose needle is a little gold star.
It's pointing somewhere… at a Fallen Star! It's Sora's star compass!
Then it can help us find every star she left for me.
The needle is pointing… at a Fallen Star. Grandma's star compass!
You were five the summer you climbed onto the station roof to wave at Kobo. Genzo nearly fainted. I pretended to scold you. — Grandma
From the bell tower you can see both villages at once. I came up here to remind myself they are one valley. — Grandma
You once asked me why the mill wheel sings. It doesn't. That was Ōta, humming. Don't tell him I told you. — Grandma
This lamp was always my favourite: it watches the whole line. If you're reading this up here, you found the Star Kite. Good girl.
The forest is older than all of us. When you feel small, come up here and be small together with it. It helps. — Grandma
Five letters, five high places. Now you've seen the valley the way I did, from above.
My favourite secret: from up here, nobody is on the other side of anything. — Grandma
For your next fish. It's lucky. Probably. Don't tell Grandpa I gave you my best lure. — Rin
Radish. Ten years' worth of stubborn. Eat it slowly. — Ōta

s: Buns for the lamp-lighter! Three of them. You know why. — Hana
A pine cone and a red maple leaf, tied with string. Tiny paw prints lead to the door.
A honey pot, very sticky, left on the step. Something large has been sitting in the garden.
My old cap. Kobo needs a junior driver on Sundays. Interested? — Genzo
A lure, radish, buns, a pine cone, honey, a cap… It isn't Grandma's empty house anymore.
It's home.
The last Fallen Star wakes in Mika's hands, and the whole sky answers.
Every star Sora ever wished on comes out at once, and the constellations remember everyone Mika met.
Her glasses on the table. Her teacups. A whole shelf of letters. It's like she only just stepped out.
I know this room! I think. It smells like toast and Sora. Mostly toast.
Did Grandma ever throw anything away? …Good. Neither will I.
Warm! It's so warm in here! Mika, I think I live here now.
Peaches, hot sugar, and an oven bigger than my room in the city. I could live in here.
So this is where Ōta hides. Gears, flour, and a truly worrying amount of pickled radish.
A timetable, a ledger and a ticking clock, all for one little train that runs to the tunnel and back.
And pictures of Kobo. And a tiny model of Kobo. Mika, I think Genzo REALLY likes Kobo.
Genzo's office. A ticking clock, a very tidy ledger, and more pictures of Kobo than of people.
…And a little model of Kobo on the desk. Of course there is.
'Sora, Genzo, Ōta, Hana. Same time next year.' …Genzo's smiling. I didn't know his face could do that.
Ōta and Hana, arm in arm, and everybody laughing! Mika, can we keep it? In the journal? Please?
Ōta and Hana, arm in arm, and all four of them laughing. …This one's going in my journal.
'Three for Ōta. He'll say he only wants one.' …Ten years of feuding, and she never crossed it out.
Ō and G… Ōta and Genzo! Two floats, tied together. They went fishing TOGETHER!
And then ten years of pickled radish. Maybe it was never really about the radish.
Ō and G, tied together with twine. Ōta and Genzo used to go fishing together.
'Genzo, age 9. I will drive this train one day.' …He did, Tamo. He really did.
Nine? Genzo was NINE once? I thought he came with the moustache.
'Genzo, age 9. I will drive this train one day.' …And he did. He really did.
Genzo at nine. I bet he already had the frown. Maybe not the moustache.
A kite? No, it has propellers. And a handlebar. And a note tied to the handlebar.
The Star Kite. It comes when you whistle and goes where my legs won't. Hold on tight, and don't tell Genzo.
Sora built a FLYING machine! Press G to fly: Space climbs, C dives, Shift goes fast, and G lands.
Press G to whistle for the kite. Space climbs, C dives, Shift goes faster, G lands. Genzo need never know.
It's so SOFT! And it's wiggling its nose at me! Mika, I don't HAVE a nose. What do I do?
The rabbit wiggles its nose at Mika. Mika, with enormous self-control, does not wiggle hers back.
Pleased to meet you, madam.
She says pleased to meet you too. I think. It might have been a threat.
The hen looks Mika over from boots to scarf, clucks once, and allows it.
Mochi opens one eye, decides Mika is acceptable, and purrs like a very small engine.
Quack! …Did I say it right? They're all looking at me. Mika, what did I SAY?
Mika waves. The ducks discuss her at length, very loudly, and then all waggle their tails at once.
The cow lifts her head, considers Mika for a long, kind moment, and goes back to her grass. Her bell says thank you.
The pig leans into the scratching with a grunt of pure joy, then flops over, completely finished with the day.
The goat sniffs Mika's sleeve, finds no snacks, and forgives her at once.
Kinako barks twice, sits, and wags so hard that the whole back half of her wags with it.
You're the one who got stuck in the hedge, aren't you?
The sheep does not deny it.
Shh. Shh! Look at the little one. Don't breathe. Okay—breathe a little.
Mika stands very still. The littlest deer steps up, sniffs her scarf, and bounds back to its mother.
